claim.why_it_matters: The printed ELEMENT column is indented to show which element each row qualifies (e.g. 'Operands must be of equal size' is a sub-entry of 'Comparison of nonnumeric operands', 'USING phrase' of 'Procedure Division header'); the transcription flattens every row to one level, unlike the neighbouring pages (737, 739, 740) which keep the nesting with   indents, so the parent of each sub-entry is lost.

verdict.reasoning: The 300 dpi render of page 738 (XVII-30) shows the ELEMENT column printed at up to five indentation levels: the two 'Procedure Division is required/optional' rows and USING phrase sit one level in; 'At least 5 operands permitted' and 'No minimum on number of operands permitted' sit two levels in under USING phrase; DECLARATIVES and END DECLARATIVES sit under Declarative procedures; the Binary and Unary operator rows sit under Arithmetic expressions; and the chain goes Simple condition > Relation condition > Relational operators > [NOT] GREATER THAN ... <=, with 'Operands must be of equal size' and 'Operands may be of unequal size' one level below 'Comparison of nonnumeric operands'. page-738.md puts every row at the left margin with no   indent. The neighbouring page 737's markdown does use   indents for the same purpose, which confirms the transcription convention exists and was dropped here. The indentation carries meaning. Without it the reader cannot tell that 'Operands must be of equal size' qualifies nonnumeric comparison only, or that the operand-count rows qualify the USING phrase. The claim quotes both sources correctly, using ellipses for leader dots. The difference is lost hierarchy, not misplaced text: every row is present and in the right order.
verdict.corrected_description: Not misplaced content. The ELEMENT column's printed indentation hierarchy (up to five levels) is flattened on page 738. Every row is present in the correct order with the correct 2ND/3RD STD values, but no row carries the   indent that page 737 uses, so which parent element each sub-entry qualifies is lost.
